The Jew of Malta. Christopher Marlowe's dark comedy-tragedy about Barabas, a wealthy Jewish merchant whose fortune is seized by the Christian Maltese governor. Driven by rage and cunning, Barabas orchestrates an elaborate revenge that spirals into chaos and his own destruction. The play explores themes of greed, religious conflict, and the consequences of unchecked ambition in a colonial Mediterranean society.

Set in Malta during Christian-Muslim conflict, with Barabas as the protagonist despite being the title's Jew, challenging audience sympathies. The play opens with Barabas secure in wealth and influence; the governor seizes his entire fortune as punishment for his religion, triggering his vengeful transformation.

Barabas schemes to pit Christian and Muslim forces against each other through manipulation, seduction, and sabotage, displaying Marlowe's fascination with cunning overreach. The play features a poisoned nunnery, a disguised false friar, and elaborate traps that recall both Renaissance intrigue and classical revenge plots.

The protagonist's downfall mirrors his own moral descent—he becomes the monster his society accused him of being. Often read as Marlowe's commentary on religious hypocrisy and the arbitrariness of power in early modern states.

The play blurs moral boundaries: Barabas is sympathetic as a victim of persecution, yet monstrous in his methods; no character escapes the play's cynicism. His daughter Abigail becomes an unwilling participant in his schemes, ultimately poisoning the nunnery where she has taken refuge.

The play's conclusion features Barabas trapped in a cauldron of boiling oil—a grotesque death befitting the play's escalating violence and moral chaos. Published in sixteen thirty-three but performed extensively in Marlowe's lifetime, it influenced the revenge tragedy tradition and remains contentious for its portrayal of Jewish characters.

Christopher Marlowe is the playwright; his only rival to Doctor Faustus in ambition and moral complexity. Revenge tragedy is the revenge plot structure that defines both character arc and theatrical spectacle. Power and corruption is the moral cost of relentless ambition and revenge. Doctor Faustus is Marlowe's other masterwork, also starring an overreacher who traffics with the forbidden. English Renaissance is the era's fascination with individual agency and transgressive desire. The Mediterranean Sea is the colonial setting that shapes Malta's religious and economic tensions.
